name: Thalassotherapy

image.caption: Outdoor Thalassotherapy Pool at Le Meridien Limassol Spa & Resort

lead: Thalassotherapy uses seawater, marine products such as algae and mud, and the seaside climate for health and wellbeing. Its name comes from the Greek for sea, and it is typically delivered in specialised coastal spa centres, with France a prominent home of the practice.

For appearance, centres offer heated seawater pools, seaweed wraps, mud packs and sea-extract massages, which users associate with hydrated, softer skin. Clinical research has mostly studied skin disorders such as psoriasis and atopic dermatitis and rheumatic conditions such as fibromyalgia.

paras: Programmes are usually multi-day stays combining immersion in heated seawater, seaweed or mud applications, massage and exposure to sea air. They are run at seaside centres, often with exercise in the water.

Reviews note that effect sizes, long-term benefits and risks still need more study. Chlorinated seawater pools have been found to contain brominated disinfection by-products, which researchers have measured in air and water.

chain: Seawater, seaweed and mud applied at a coastal spa
Minerals and osmotic effects act on skin
angle.text: Centres present seawater and marine products as skin-conditioning and relaxing treatments, and studies of skin conditions report symptom improvement that may show as calmer skin.

lead: Thalassotherapy is the therapeutic use of seawater, sea products such as algae, mud and sand, and the coastal climate. The term was coined in 1867 by physician Joseph de la Bonnardiere, according to Grokipedia, and ISO 17680:2015 defines it as the use of marine resources under medical supervision at coastal sites. [1][1]

People use it for skin and body care: heated seawater baths, seaweed wraps, mud packs and sea-extract massages. Reviews say hypertonic saline water interacts with skin cells and nerve receptors, and seaweed supplies antioxidants and polysaccharides such as fucoidan. [1][2]

A 2025 narrative review identified 16 clinical studies, mostly of skin disorders (psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, vitiligo) and rheumatic disease, and reported improved severity and quality of life, strongest in psoriasis and fibromyalgia. [3] Wikipedia states that there is no scientific evidence that it is effective, reflecting differing assessments across sources. [4]

paras: Thalassotherapy differs from balneotherapy, which uses inland mineral spring water, and from hydrotherapy, which uses ordinary water. Typical treatments include immersion in heated seawater pools, marine mud and seaweed wraps, and sea-extract massage, with coastal air as part of the programme. [1]
Seawater is about 3.5% salt, mainly sodium and chloride with magnesium, sulfate, calcium and potassium. [1]

Writers trace sea bathing for health to Egyptians, Greeks and Romans. Wikipedia credits Dr Richard Russell with fuelling the 18th-century seaside craze, and notes heated saltwater public baths in the 19th century. [1][4] France became a leading centre in the 20th century. [1] Wikipedia also notes that Lydia Sarfati introduced seaweed skin treatments to the United States. [4]

A 2018 review proposed that sodium- and chloride-rich water modifies cellular osmotic pressure in keratinocytes and stimulates skin nerve receptors via Piezo channels. [2] A 2011 paper asked whether thalassotherapy is simply a type of climatotherapy. [5]
Chlorinated seawater swimming pools have been found to produce brominated disinfection by-products, measured in water and air. [6][7] A 2025 review states that risks still need assessment. [3]

A 2008 review of climatotherapy for psoriasis reports controlled studies of thalassotherapy at the Dead Sea and Black Sea. [8] A randomised trial of 46 women with fibromyalgia compared aerobic exercise in the sea with a pool, and a 2005 randomised trial found a spa programme combining thalassotherapy, exercise and education improved symptoms and quality of life. [9][10] A 2009 meta-analysis examined hydrotherapy for fibromyalgia. [11] The 2025 review found the strongest evidence in psoriasis and fibromyalgia and called for work on effect size and long-term benefit. [3] No trials of cosmetic anti-ageing outcomes are listed.
